Swift and the app’s front door

  1. Read a nullable Swift value
  2. Follow a struct copy and a class reference
  3. Start an app and identify a scene
  4. Separate a Task from an awaited call

Read a nullable Swift value

Swift's let binds a constant and var permits reassignment. An optional explicitly represents either a wrapped value or its absence. Unwrap it before using a nonoptional operation. A forced unwrap transfers the missing-value check to a runtime trap.

Worked example

A route contains a note ID as text. Int("17") yields an optional containing 17. Int("river") yields nil. Use guard let id = Int(raw) else { return } before loading the note, and decide how the screen presents an invalid route.

Try it

Is an empty note list the same state as failing to parse the requested ID?

Compare your answer

No. Empty is a valid collection value. A missing or invalid route is a different input outcome and should be handled at the navigation boundary.

Source · The Swift Programming Language · The Basics

Follow a struct copy and a class reference

Swift structures have value semantics: changing a copied value does not change the original value. Classes have reference semantics and can be shared by multiple variables. A struct can contain a reference property, in which case copying the struct copies that reference as part of its value.

Worked example

With struct Draft { var title: String }, set b = a, then b.title = "Lake". The title of a stays River. If Draft is a class and both variables point to the same instance, mutating b.title is visible through a.

Try it

A struct stores a class-based Editor. After copying the struct, do both copies see a change made to that same Editor?

Compare your answer

Yes. The copied properties refer to one Editor instance. Use an independent value representation or intentionally create a new editor when isolation is required.

Source · The Swift Programming Language · Structures and Classes

Start an app and identify a scene

The @main App type is the entry point for a SwiftUI app. Its body describes scenes, and a WindowGroup can host separate instances of a window's content. A process may own several scene sessions with different selections and lifecycle states.

Worked example

A notes app's WindowGroup opens a root list. One window edits note 17 and another edits 29. Both can share the persisted note repository while keeping their navigation selection attached to the individual scene.

Try it

A single global selectedNote changes both windows when one user navigates. What should move?

Compare your answer

Move selection to scene- or view-owned state. Keep genuinely shared data, such as saved notes, in a separate shared model.

Source · Apple · SwiftUI App

Separate a Task from an awaited call

An async function may suspend. Calling it with await does not by itself start independent concurrent work or move CPU-heavy code off an actor. Task creates unstructured work with a handle and can inherit the surrounding actor context. Actor isolation governs access to mutable state.

Worked example

A main-actor action creates Task { await refresh() }. When refresh awaits network data other main-actor work may proceed. Synchronously decoding a huge document on that same actor can still block input. Identify the executor or isolation of each expensive step.

Try it

Two taps start independent refreshes. Why can an older response still replace a newer one despite main-actor writes?

Compare your answer

Serialization of individual state updates does not impose request order across suspension. Cancel superseded work or validate an operation generation before publishing it.

Source · The Swift Programming Language · Concurrency
